main.title: The pinhole
main.question: How can a hole make a picture?

transcript.text: This camera has no lens.
No glass. No battery. No sensor.
Just a hole, a quarter of a millimetre wide.
So how does a hole make a picture?
Hold a piece of film up to a tree. Light from each point of the tree lands on every part of the film.
So every part of the film sees the whole tree at once. All the light is there. The picture is not.
Now put a wall with a small hole between them. Most of the light is stopped.
Each part of the film can see only one point of the tree: the one in line with the hole. That is all a picture is.
It is upside down, and left and right are swapped, because the rays cross in the hole. Move a point up the tree and its picture moves down.
People have known this for about 2,400 years. For most of them, nobody could make the picture stay.

Make it smaller and the picture gets sharper, and dimmer: the exposure gets longer.
For this camera, 28.7 mm from hole to film, the sharpest hole is about a quarter of a millimetre.
Smaller still and it gets worse again. Light spreads out as it squeezes through a tiny hole.
So a pinhole has a best size. The picture can never be sharper than that, which is why a lens was worth inventing.
1544. Gemma Frisius, Leuven. He watches an eclipse of the sun safely inside a dark room, and prints a picture of the room the year after.

chapters.title: What a curve of glass does

In 1568, Daniele Barbaro put a glass made for spectacles in the hole of a dark room.

In 1611, Johannes Kepler worked out why: how a lens bends light into a picture.
Light from one point of the tree spreads out over the whole lens.
The curved glass bends each ray, the outer ones most, so they all meet again.

main.title: Film
main.question: How does a strip of plastic remember a picture?

chapters.title: Colour is three films in one

transcript.text: This is the film for your camera: a strip of plastic, 35 millimetres wide.
Light touches it for about a three-hundredth of a second.
Weeks later the picture is still there. How does a strip of plastic remember a picture?
Most people guess the light draws the picture there and then, as on a phone.
If so, you could open the back and look. You would see plain film.
People did try light alone. By 1727, Johann Schulze had shown that silver salts darken in light.
About 1800, Thomas Wedgwood coated paper with them and let the sun print shadows on it.
But in a camera it failed, and in daylight his pictures went dark all over.
Too slow, and it never stops.
Film is cleverer. On the plastic is a coat of gelatin: Richard Maddox's idea, in 1871.
In the gelatin lie crystals of silver salt, each about a thousandth of a millimetre across.
When light strikes a crystal, a few atoms of silver gather into a speck.
About four atoms are enough: far too few to see. But the crystal is marked.
Bright parts of the scene mark many crystals, dark parts few. That pattern is the picture.
In the dark, the film goes into a bath called developer.
Developer turns each marked crystal, all of it, into black silver, and leaves the rest.
A few atoms become billions: the light's work, multiplied about a billion times.
Daguerre's silver plates, made public in 1839, worked this way: mercury fumes brought the picture out.
So did Talbot's paper, in 1841: an hour's wait became a minute or two.
But unmarked crystals can still darken. In 1839 John Herschel showed that a salt, hypo, dissolves them: fixing.
Developed and fixed, the picture is plain silver, and light cannot change it.
Where the scene was brightest there is most silver, so the film is darkest.
A white cloud comes out black, a dark doorway clear. It is a negative.
Shine light through it onto fresh paper, and backwards turns backwards again: a positive.
Herschel chose both words. One Talbot negative could print many positives.
Colour film is three films in one: one catches blue light, one green, one red.
In developing, each layer's silver makes a dye; then the silver is washed out.
Three dye pictures are left, in backwards colours, under an orange tint.
Layered colour film went on sale in 1935,
and colour negatives for prints in 1942.
Now a sum. Count light in steps: one step is double, or half.
Colour negative film forgives one step too little, and three steps too much.
One step under is half. Three steps over is two times two times two: eight.
Eight divided by a half is sixteen: the window is sixteen times wide.
That is why your camera needs only one shutter speed and three holes.
The box gives the film's speed. ISO 400 needs a quarter of the light ISO 100 needs.
With ISO 400, your camera can snap from full sun down to bright cloud.
After each picture you wind it back into the film's shell, into the dark.
Keep the back shut: until it is developed, film goes on catching light.
Posting film away is old: in 1888 the first Kodak went back to its factory, camera and all.
So how does plastic remember? Light marks crystals of silver salt. Developing makes the marks a picture.
Look. Hold an old negative up to a window: the darkest parts were the brightest things.
Try. Leave a key on dark paper in the sun: see how slow light alone is.
Next, lesson four: why do camera numbers go eight, eleven, sixteen?
Every picture here is drawn or simulated. No photograph has been taken with this camera yet.

main.question: How do you make a piece of plastic move that fast, the same way every time?

chapters.title: A window that passes a hole
Why a click and not a spring

transcript.text: Press the rocker. Light reaches the film for about a three-hundredth of a second.
Three hundred of those would fit into one second.
And the shutter is one piece of printed plastic, with no bought spring.
So how do you make plastic move that fast, the same way every time?
Most people guess: a strong spring, and a quick, careful finger.
But fingers differ. A slow press and a quick one would give different pictures.
And this camera has no strong spring. The answer is a click.
In 1839 a picture took minutes. The shutter was a cap: take it off, count, put it back.
Then plates got faster, and no hand was quick enough.
In June 1878, Eadweard Muybridge set twelve cameras beside a racetrack.
Wires across the track were broken as the horses ran past. Each wire fired one camera's shutter.
The pictures showed a galloping horse with all four feet off the ground.
In the 1880s, a simple fast shutter was a plate with a hole, dropped past the lens.
Yours is the same idea, swung instead of dropped.
The blade (teal in these pictures) turns on a peg. It has one window.
At rest, solid plastic covers the lens. Press, and the blade swings across.
For an instant the window is over the lens. Then solid plastic again.
The next press swings it back the other way. One press, one picture.
The blade's own rim is springy. A tooth on the rim sits in a notch.
Press the rocker and the tooth pushes up the notch's slope. Nothing moves yet.
Your finger pushes harder, up to about 2.3 newtons, by the model. Then the tooth jumps out.
All that push is let go at once. Finger and blade fly together through the swing.
Like snapping your fingers: press until they slip, and the snap is always quick.
Clockwork did this job in 1910: the Compur shutter timed itself, up to a two-hundred-and-fiftieth of a second.
Without the click, the blade would only go as fast as your finger.
Now a sum. Without the click, pushed slowly, the model gives about a twenty-eighth of a second.
With the click, about a three-hundred-and-twenty-second. 322 divided by 28 is about 11.5.
In steps of light, 11.5 lies between 8 and 16: about three and a half steps.
Full sun, small dot is already half a step over. Add three and a half: four steps.
Film forgives three. So a slow press spoils the picture. The click saves it.
No two presses are quite alike: by the model, about half a step either way.
Printers differ too. A print with fatter walls has a stiffer rim, so a faster snap.
From the thinnest printer's parts to the fattest, the model's time runs from 1/176 to 1/423.
Judging the sky by eye is good to about one step. The shutter is steadier.
Press the rocker only halfway, to its middle click, and the window stops over the lens.
Now it stays open. Count, then press on down. That is a time picture.
By a window, small dot, ISO 400: count one. With the lamps on, five.
Stand the camera on something steady. No hand holds still for a count.
In your kit, the blade drops onto a peg in the front plate. No spring to lose.
So: the finger only loads the click. The click lets go at the same force every time.
Look: try to snap your fingers slowly. However you press, the snap is quick.

transcript.text: After each picture you turn the green knob, and one picture's length of film moves.
Too little, and two pictures overlap. Too much, and film is wasted.
There is no motor and no chip. How does the camera know it has moved exactly one picture?
Most people guess: count turns of the knob. One turn, one picture.
But film winds onto a roll, and the roll grows fatter with every turn.
A fatter roll takes in more film each turn.
Empty, one turn takes in a little under one picture. Full, it takes in about one and two-thirds.
So turns cannot count pictures. The camera must measure the film itself.
Look at the film's edges. A row of holes runs along each, top and bottom.
About 1892, in Thomas Edison's laboratory, William Dickson settled on film 35 millimetres wide, with holes down both edges.
It was for moving pictures: teeth in the holes pulled it along exactly.
On today's film the holes are 4.75 millimetres apart.
In 1913 Oskar Barnack designed a small camera that ran this film sideways, for still pictures.
His picture was 36 by 24 millimetres. Yours is exactly the same size.
It went on sale in 1925, as the Leica.
One picture is 36 millimetres long, and the gap after it 2: 38 millimetres.
And eight holes, 4.75 apart, make exactly 38 millimetres. Eight holes, one picture.
So the camera counts holes, not turns. That is the blue frame wheel's job.
It has eight teeth, and they sit in the holes along the film's top edge.
The wheel does not pull the film. The film, moving, turns the wheel.
Eight holes pass, the wheel turns once, and the arrow on the frame wheel comes home.
The camera does not stop you. You stop when the arrow comes round.
Each tooth tapers, so it finds its hole.
By the model, with thin film or thick, no tooth touches a hole's edge.
To load, you wind the whole film out of its shell onto the red spool.
That takes about 25 turns for 24 pictures, 33 for 36.
Then, after each picture, the green knob winds it back into the shell.
Why backwards? The shell is dark inside: pictures already taken are safe in it.
If the back opens by accident, only pictures not yet taken are lost.
The shell you can load in daylight came in 1934.
Now a sum. One turn of a roll takes in its distance round: two times 3.14 times its radius.
The red spool empty: radius 5.9 millimetres. One turn: about 37 millimetres, just under one picture.
Full after 36 pictures: radius 10.1. One turn: about 63 millimetres.
63 divided by 37 is 1.7. The last turn moves 1.7 times the film of the first.
The same happens in the film's shell: the roll the green knob winds grows with every picture.
Same knob, same turn, very different lengths. Only the holes stay the same.
In your kit, the frame wheel lies in a fork on the back, beside a round post.
Close the back and its teeth come down on the film's top edge.
After the last picture, wind the green knob until the arrow stops. Then three more turns.
Now all the film is in its shell, and the back can come off.

So how does it know? It counts holes: eight holes, 38 millimetres, one turn of the wheel.

One picture is 36 millimetres long, and the gap after it 2: 38 millimetres.

17

And eight holes, 4.75 apart, make exactly 38 millimetres. Eight holes, one picture.

18

So the camera counts holes, not turns. That is the blue frame wheel's job.

19
00:01:39.167 --> 00:01:43.165
It has eight teeth, and they sit in the holes along the film's top edge.

20

The wheel does not pull the film. The film, moving, turns the wheel.

21

Eight holes pass, the wheel turns once, and the arrow on the frame wheel comes home.

22

The camera does not stop you. You stop when the arrow comes round.

23
00:01:57.567 --> 00:02:00.153
Each tooth tapers, so it finds its hole.

24
00:02:00.567 --> 00:02:04.848
By the model, with thin film or thick, no tooth touches a hole's edge.

25
00:02:05.267 --> 00:02:09.115
To load, you wind the whole film out of its shell onto the red spool.

26
00:02:09.533 --> 00:02:14.686
That takes about 25 turns for 24 pictures, 33 for 36.

27
00:02:15.100 --> 00:02:19.216
Then, after each picture, the green knob winds it back into the shell.

28
00:02:19.633 --> 00:02:24.643
Why backwards? The shell is dark inside: pictures already taken are safe in it.

29
00:02:25.067 --> 00:02:29.730
If the back opens by accident, only pictures not yet taken are lost.

30
00:02:30.133 --> 00:02:33.696
The shell you can load in daylight came in 1934.

31
00:02:34.100 --> 00:02:41.139
Now a sum. One turn of a roll takes in its distance round: two times 3.14 times its radius.

32
00:02:41.567 --> 00:02:49.746
The red spool empty: radius 5.9 millimetres. One turn: about 37 millimetres, just under one picture.

33
00:02:50.167 --> 00:02:56.721
Full after 36 pictures: radius 10.1. One turn: about 63 millimetres.

34
00:02:57.133 --> 00:03:05.378

35
00:03:05.800 --> 00:03:11.305
The same happens in the film's shell: the roll the green knob winds grows with every picture.

36
00:03:11.733 --> 00:03:16.374
Same knob, same turn, very different lengths. Only the holes stay the same.

37
00:03:16.800 --> 00:03:21.359
In your kit, the frame wheel lies in a fork on the back, beside a round post.

38
00:03:21.767 --> 00:03:25.231
Close the back and its teeth come down on the film's top edge.

39
00:03:25.633 --> 00:03:31.195
After the last picture, wind the green knob until the arrow stops. Then three more turns.

40

Now all the film is in its shell, and the back can come off.

While you wind, keep a hand off the red knob, and never force either knob.

00:03:40.167 --> 00:03:45.633

main.question: How can a box full of gaps be dark inside?

transcript.text: Two knobs, a spinning frame wheel, a back that comes off. This camera is full of gaps.
Inside lies film that a moment of daylight would ruin.
So how can a box full of gaps be dark inside?
Most people guess it must be sealed tight, like a jar with its lid screwed on.
It is not tight anywhere. Each knob has over half a millimetre of room, so it can turn.
The back sits in its groove with room to spare. Air could get through every gap.
Air goes round corners. Light, mostly, does not. That is the whole trick.
Light travels in straight lines. About a thousand years ago, Ibn al-Haytham showed it with lamps and one opening.
Screen one lamp, and only its spot goes out. Each spot came straight from its own lamp.
So a gap is harmless if no straight line runs through it to the film.
Here is the joint where the back meets the body, cut through.
A ridge on the back stands in a groove in the body, with a step on each side.
Light coming in must turn one corner, then another, then another.
The ridge reaches almost two millimetres in, so even a back left a little open has no straight way in.
The knobs work the same way. Each head lies flat on the body's top.
A ring on the stem runs in a channel, and a block on the back closes the slot behind.
The film's own shell keeps dark the same way.
In 1934, film came in a metal shell you could load in daylight. Its slot is lined with soft fibres.
How do you check a camera nobody has printed? You fire light at the computer model.
Rays leave the film in every direction. A way out is also a way in.
Twenty-one cases: the shutter loose or pushed, a thin print, the frame wheel up and down.
Sixty-nine million rays. Not one reached the outside.
Does the test work at all? Hold the shutter open, and 251 rays escape.
Every one leaves through the lens's opening, where light is meant to come in.
So the test can find light. Shut, it found none.
Straight lines are half the story. Light also bounces, and no plastic is perfectly black.
Now a sum. The model lets every surface send back 30 percent: more than black plastic does.
One bounce keeps 0.3. Two bounces: 0.3 times 0.3, which is 0.09.
Three bounces: 0.027. That is about one part in 37.
Five bounces: about one part in 400. And most bounced light goes the wrong way.
Every corner divides the light again. That is why it is called a light trap.
In your kit, press the back on until both ends click. A back left standing off is the biggest risk.
The back is drawn light grey. Even a grey back keeps the inside dark, because every gap is a light trap.
Open the back only when the film is wound home into its shell.
Proved? Not yet. Rays in a computer are not light on film.
The real test waits for a printed camera: a loaded roll, lens covered, an hour in the sun.
If a frame comes back fogged, the fog's shape will point to the gap.
So the box stays dark: no straight line runs through any gap, and every bounce throws light away.
Look. In a dark room, find where light shows round a closed door. Where does the gap run straight?
Try. Make a light trap from a shoebox and some card, and test it with a torch.

main.question: Same camera, same film. Why are some pictures better than others?

main.hook: Two people, the same camera, the same roll, the same afternoon. One comes home with pictures people stop to look at. xref.idea: With one speed, three dots and fixed focus, a good picture is choices: the light, the distance, the middle of the frame.

main.title: Your phone's camera

main.hook: Open your phone's camera and every piece of the CURVE 35 is in there, shrunk to the size of a pea: the dark box, the hole, the lens, the shutter, the thing that catches light. They just work differently. Here they all are again, and the one idea that ties them together.

maker.question: If a printer can make any shape, why isn't this camera just any shape?

maker.hook: Every part of this camera comes off an ordinary desktop printer: no supports, no brim, no sanding. That isn't luck. A printer lays a hot line of plastic thinner than a pencil lead, one layer at a time, and it never hits a drawn width exactly. Every hook, gap and spring in the files is drawn around those two facts.

xref.idea: A printer lays plastic a line and a layer at a time and never hits a drawn size exactly, so every shape is drawn around that.
